title: The Fastest Way to Board a Plane Feels Like the Slowest
beats: What is the fastest way to board a plane? Not funneled like cattle
Monkey brains and boarding groups; back-to-front fills a cylinder, intuitive
Obvious, sensible, easy solutions are often terrible; back-to-front is what most airlines use
Watch it: first passenger stows, everyone behind waits
Bags cause most delay; full-stop stow named
Name the wanted events: pullaways (one queue becomes two) and parallels (simultaneous stowing)
If you were malicious: front-to-back, small groups, maximally slow
Real planes: first class boards first, front to back, so airlines start with the slowest method
Economic incentives and loyalty points explain why airlines group people
Random boarding is faster than orderly groups: doing nothing beats the something
Real simulations show seat shuffle matters little next to bags; only a smidge faster
Most airlines use back-to-front or window-middle-aisle
Idealized physics world: cellular-automaton people give the perfect interleaved order
Descend back to real people: families, group numbers, complaints
Compromise: one side, every other row, alternate; keeps families and groups, still faster
Reaching for perfection we come up short but get closer

metrics.misconception: yes: intuitive back-to-front is bad, and the simple window-middle-aisle improvement is overstated (0:31, 4:25)
metrics.brute_force: yes 2:10: design the worst method deliberately to expose what matters
metrics.examples: ~5 boarding methods compared: back-to-front, front-to-back, random, window-middle-aisle, perfect, compromise; each judged by pullaways/parallels
metrics.ending: Practical compromise rotating the ideal into a usable group scheme; moral about approaching perfection

principles.6: confirmed: worst-case design at 2:10 reveals the mechanism
principles.7: confirmed: same watching of queues repeatedly reveals bags as the cause (0:49-1:38)

principles.11: confirmed: bags, then terms, then bad, random, WMA, ideal, compromise

new_moves.name: design-the-worst
new_moves.what: Ask the learner to be malicious and maximize the problem to reveal mechanism

new_moves.name: ideal-then-descend
new_moves.what: Show the perfect idealized solution, then compromise toward reality

new_moves.name: toy-demo-disclaimer
new_moves.what: Admit the animation is simplified and real simulation says otherwise

theory: Grey picks one hidden cause (bag stowing blocks the aisle), names its good and bad events, then scores every boarding scheme against those two names. Designing the worst case and then the perfect case brackets reality, so the real compromise is understood, not just announced.
velocity: Scene builder: queue sim with highlighted pullaway and parallel events as a reusable scoring overlay
Orchestrator: playbook 'bracket it': worst case, random baseline, ideal, then realistic compromise
Voice: plant presenter-was-wrong beat when a tidy simplified sim misleads
Learner model: ask learner to propose a malicious design before revealing mechanism
Evals: check every candidate method is scored with the same two terms
quote: subtract malice and add thinking to this problem
